- **The one-dimensional instance.** For $n=1$ the data are $M=m>0$,
$K=k\in\mathbb R$ and $J=f$, and the equation is $m\,x''+k\,x=f(t)$, which is
exactly the forced scalar model $m\,x''+0\cdot x'+k\,x=f$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with $c=0$. To identify this
with the physical scalar class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] clause (f), require a
length-valued position or displacement coordinate, $\gamma_1=\ell$, read
in a fixed inertial frame, take configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, and
restrict to an open time interval. Reconstructing dimensional data from
clause (a), the scalar $\mathsf M$ is then a mass in kilograms,
$\mathsf K$ a stiffness in newtons per metre, and $\mathsf J$ a force in
newtons; the numerical SI coefficients correspond to that definition's
$(m,0,k,f)$. In particular this includes $k>0$ and constant, vanishing or
sinusoidal force. With this same length-coordinate identification, at a
scalar strict minimum the small-oscillation stiffness is $U''(x_*)\ge0$;
the free model is the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] when
$U''(x_*)>0$, and the free zero-stiffness model when $U''(x_*)=0$.
For an angular coordinate the dimensional $\mathsf M$ and $\mathsf J$
instead have the units of rotational inertia and torque; the mathematical
scalar equation still applies, but the physical mass-and-force
identification requires a separately declared change to a length coordinate. An isolated strict minimum can have zero Hessian (for example $U(x)=x^4$); the accuracy of
that approximation in time and amplitude is not part of the present item.
uses.reason: Remarks identify the n=1 length-coordinate model with the harmonic law only when U″>0 and already distinguish angular inertia/torque. The extra sine supplier and angular comparison preserve that identification.

uses.affected_use:
[L1] General theory ([[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]] clause 1,
[[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]],
[[pthm-cm04-damped-decay-and-stability]]): with $m>0,k>0,c\ge0$ the motions
are the three families according to the sign of $\Delta=c^{2}-4mk$, with
coefficients $A=(v_{0}-\lambda_{-}x_{0})/(\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-})$,
$B=(\lambda_{+}x_{0}-v_{0})/(\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-})$ for $\Delta>0$,
$A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}-\lambda x_{0}$ for $\Delta=0$, and $A=x_{0}$,
$B=(v_{0}+\gamma x_{0})/\omega$ for $\Delta<0$; the motions extend to
$\mathbb R$; the energy satisfies $E'=-c\,x'^{2}$; and for $c>0$ the
decay bounds of the three cases hold with $r_{0}=\sqrt{x_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}$.

3.1 Energy. With $m=k=1$ the energy is $E=\tfrac12v^{2}+\tfrac12x^{2}$, and $E(0)=\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot1=\tfrac12$ J in all three cases. By [L1] the identity $E'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}$ holds along each motion, so $E'(t)<0$ exactly when $x'(t)\ne0$. In the first case the exceptional times are $t=2\pi n/\sqrt3$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$, by the sine zero set and the positive exponential factor in step 2.1. In the second and third cases the derivative vanishes only at $t=0$ and $E'(t)<0$ for every $t\ne0$. In particular no motion here is a constant-energy motion other than the rest motion, consistent with clause 2 of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra]
uses.reason: L1 and Verification 3.1 use E′=−c v² with c=1,2,5>0; strict negativity is restricted to nonzero velocity. Its current L3 correctly assigns velocity units to critical B and step 3.1 uses all integer exceptional times.

**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$,
the spring constant $k>0$ of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]], and a **drag
coefficient** $c\ge0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-1}$, read in kilograms per
second ([[def-cm01-units]]). The model's force law is declared through the
additive composition of force contributions, in the sense of clause (v) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read in one coordinate:
$$F(x,v)=-k\,x-c\,v .$$

The **damped oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model with this force
law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0,$$
and its data $(m,c,k,0)$ are oscillator-type data in the sense of clause (f)
of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The model is
autonomous and depends on the velocity; it is **undamped** when $c=0$, in
which case it is exactly the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]],
and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

**(ii) Potential presentation with a residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of
[[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] together with the **residual force**
$$d(t,x,v)=-c\,v,$$
in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is therefore
the function $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of clause (d), defined
along every motion; the drag force is not presented through a potential and
the model is not a global potential model when $c>0$.
uses.reason: Postulate (i)-(ii) use the unchanged k>0 restoring law and U=kx²/2 to add −cv; c=0 is still the harmonic model. The angular pendulum comparison is not a premise.

uses.affected_use:
1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.
uses.reason: Statement clause 1 and Proof 1.1 identify the c=0 equation with the unchanged harmonic model m x″+kx=0. The newly explicit angular comparison supplies no premise to this identification; assigned review follows.

1. **Motion bounds.** For every motion $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the model
   with datum $(0,x_{0},v_{0})$ and phase norm $r_{0}$ the following bounds
   hold for all $t\ge0$, with the coefficients $A,B$ of the
   classification of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]:
   - $\Delta>0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda_{+}\rvert\lvert
     A\rvert+\lvert\lambda_{-}\rvert\lvert B\rvert\bigr)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert t)e^{\lambda t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda A+B\rvert+\lvert\lambda
     B\rvert t\bigr)e^{\lambda t}$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\omega
     B-\gamma A\rvert+\lvert\gamma B+\omega A\rvert\bigr)e^{-\gamma t}$;
   and there are constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$, depending only on $(m,k,c)$, with
   $$\lvert x(t)\rvert\le C_{1}r_{0},\qquad\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le C_{2}r_{0} \qquad(t\ge0),$$
   for the numerical SI coordinate values; equivalently the corresponding
   physical position and velocity are bounded by $(1\,\mathrm m)C_{1}r_{0}$
   and $(1\,\mathrm{m/s})C_{2}r_{0}$. Here $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ are dimensionless
   constants in the normalized SI coordinates and depend only on the
   numerical values of $(m,k,c)$ in the units declared by
   [[def-cm01-units]].
2. **Convergence.** For every maximal motion, $x(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)\to0$ as

3. **Strictly damped case $c>0$.** For every $\Omega>0$ the following hold:
  every motion is bounded on $[0,\infty)$; and
   $x(t)-x_{p}(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$. Moreover
   $x_{p}$ is the unique motion with datum
   $(t_{0},x_{p}(t_{0}),x_{p}'(t_{0}))$ for any $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$. The
   amplitude function $\Omega\mapsto A(\Omega)$ has the following shape when $f_0\ne0$: if
   $c^{2}<2mk$ it is strictly increasing on $(0,\Omega_{*})$ and strictly
   decreasing on $(\Omega_{*},\infty)$, so has its unique maximum there, with
   $$\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^{2}}{2m^{2}}},\qquad A(\Omega_{*})=\frac{2m\lvert f_{0}\rvert}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}};$$
   if $c^{2}\ge2mk$ it is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and does not
   attain a maximum on the declared positive-frequency domain. Its continuous
   extension to $\Omega=0$ has its maximum there. For $f_0=0$ the amplitude is
   identically zero on the domain, so every frequency has the same value.
4. **Undamped case away from resonance.** For $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ every motion is bounded on $\mathbb R$.
5. **Undamped resonance.** For $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}\neq0$
   the motion $x_{p}(t)=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$ is unbounded

   bounded.

   every $\Omega>0$ is admissible; for $c=0$ the exceptional frequency is

   clauses 3 and 4 hold for $c>0$, and for $c=0$ away from $\Omega=\omega_{0}$,
